communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I consider that a man's brain originally is like a little empty attic, and you have to stock it with such furniture as you choose. A fool takes in all the lumber of every sort that he comes across, so that the knowledge which might be useful to him gets crowded out, or at best is jumbled up with a lot of other things so that he has a difficulty in laying his hands upon it. Now the skilful workman is very careful indeed as to what he takes into his brain-attic. He will have nothing but the tools which may help him in doing his work, but of these he has a large assortment, and all in the most perfect order. It is a mistake to think that that little room has elastic walls and can distend to any extent. events.label: Sherlock Holmes explains how he inferred a client's origin from observation and deduction

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Quite so. I have a kind of intuition that way. Now and again a case turns up which is a little more complex. Then I have to bustle about and see things with my own eyes. You see I have a lot of special knowledge which I apply to the problem, and which facilitates matters wonderfully. Those rules of deduction laid down in that article which aroused your scorn, are invaluable to me in practical work. Observation with me is second nature. You appeared to be surprised when I told you, on our first meeting, that you had come from Afghanistan. Nothing of the sort. I knew you came from Afghanistan. From long habit the train of thoughts ran so swiftly through my mind, that I arrived at the conclusion without being conscious of intermediate steps. There were such steps, however. The train of reasoning ran, 'Here is a gentleman of a medical type, but with the air of a military man. Clearly an army doctor, then. He has just come from the tropics, for his face is dark, and that is not the natural tint of his skin, for his wrists are fair. He has undergone hardship and sickness, as his haggard face says clearly. His left arm has been injured. He holds it in a stiff and unnatural manner. Where in the tropics could an English army doctor have seen much hardship and got his arm wounded?' The whole train of thought did not occupy a second. I then remarked that you came from Afghanistan, and you were astonished.

communicates.content: No doubt you think that you are complimenting me in comparing me to Dupin. Now, in my opinion, Dupin was a very inferior fellow. That trick of his of breaking in on his friends' thoughts with an apropos remark after a quarter of an hour's silence is really very showy and superficial. He had some analytical genius, no doubt; but he was by no means such a phenomenon as Poe appeared to imagine. Lecoq was a miserable bungler; he had only one thing to recommend him, and that was his energy. That book made me positively ill. The question was how to identify an unknown prisoner. I could have done it in twenty-four hours. Lecoq took six months or so. It might be made a text-book for detectives to teach them what to avoid.

There is no crime to detect, or, at most, some bungling villainy with a motive so transparent that even a Scotland Yard official can see through it.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: How did you word your inquiries?

events.label: Gregson explains the wording of the inquiries.

communicates.speaker: gregson
communicates.content: We simply detailed the circumstances, and said that we should be glad of any information which could help us.

events.label: Lestrade reappears in the hall from the front room rubbing his hands self-satisfiedly

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: I have just made a discovery of the highest importance, and one which would have been overlooked had I not made a careful examination of the walls.

events.label: Lestrade shows the wall inscription to the others

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: This was overlooked because it was in the darkest corner of the room, and no one thought of looking there. The murderer has written it with his or her own blood. See this smear where it has trickled down the wall! That disposes of the idea of suicide anyhow. Why was that corner chosen to write it on? I will tell you. See that candle on the mantelpiece. It was lit at the time, and if it was lit this corner would be the brightest instead of the darkest portion of the wall.

events.label: Gregson responds to Lestrade's explanation

communicates.speaker: gregson
communicates.content: And what does it mean now that you have found it?

events.label: Lestrade says the writer was going to write the female name Rachel and that a woman named Rachel has something to do with the case

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: Mean? Why, it means that the writer was going to put the female name Rachel, but was disturbed before he or she had time to finish. You mark my words, when this case comes to be cleared up you will find that a woman named Rachel has something to do with it. It's all very well for you to laugh, Mr. Sherlock Holmes. You may be very smart and clever, but the old hound is the best, when all is said and done.

events.label: Sherlock Holmes apologizes and says he will examine the room

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I really beg your pardon! You certainly have the credit of being the first of us to find this out, and, as you say, it bears every mark of having been written by the other participant in last night's mystery. I have not had time to examine this room yet, but with your permission I shall do so now.

events.label: Sherlock Holmes examines the room with a tape measure and magnifying glass
Holmes remarks that genius is an infinite capacity for taking pains and applies it to detective work

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: They say that genius is an infinite capacity for taking pains. It's a very bad definition, but it does apply to detective work.

events.label: Gregson and Lestrade watch Holmes's manoeuvres with curiosity and contempt

communicates.speaker: gregson
communicates.content: What do you think of it, sir?

events.label: Holmes declines to interfere and says he may later help with the investigation

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It would be robbing you of the credit of the case if I was to presume to help you. You are doing so well now that it would be a pity for anyone to interfere. If you will let me know how your investigations go, I shall be happy to give you any help I can.

events.label: Holmes asks to speak to the constable who found the body and requests his name and address

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: In the meantime I should like to speak to the constable who found the body. Can you give me his name and address?

events.label: Lestrade identifies John Rance and gives his address

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: John Rance. He is off duty now. You will find him at 46, Audley Court, Kennington Park Gate.

events.label: Holmes notes John Rance's address and decides to go look him up with Watson
Holmes states that murder has been done and describes the murderer

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There has been murder done, and the murderer was a man. He was more than six feet high, was in the prime of life, had small feet for his height, wore coarse, square-toed boots and smoked a Trichinopoly cigar. He came here with his victim in a four-wheeled cab, which was drawn by a horse with three old shoes and one new one on his off fore leg. In all probability the murderer had a florid face, and the finger-nails of his right hand were remarkably long. These are only a few indications, but they may assist you.

events.label: Lestrade and Gregson react with an incredulous smile
Lestrade asks how the man was murdered

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: If this man was murdered, how was it done?

events.label: Holmes answers that the murder was by poison and leaves

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Poison. 'Rache,' is the German for 'revenge'; so don't lose your time looking for Miss Rachel.

events.label: Holmes leaves No. 3, Lauriston Gardens and goes to the telegraph office
Holmes dispatches a long telegram
Holmes hails a cab and orders the driver to take them to the address given by Lestrade

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: take us to the address given us by Lestrade

events.label: Holmes explains his deductions about the cab, the two visitors, and the night arrival

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There is nothing like first hand evidence; as a matter of fact, my mind is entirely made up upon the case, but still we may as well learn all that is to be learned. The cab had made two ruts close to the curb, and because there had been no rain for a week until last night, the wheels must have been there during the night. The cab must have brought those two individuals to the house.

events.label: Watson questions Holmes about the deductions

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: You amaze me, Holmes. Surely you are not as sure as you pretend to be of all those particulars which you gave. But how about the other man's height? And his age? The finger nails and the Trichinopoly? And the florid face?

events.label: Holmes answers that there is no room for a mistake

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There's no room for a mistake.

events.label: Holmes explains how he inferred the other man's height

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The height of a man can be told from the length of his stride. I had this fellow's stride both on the clay outside and on the dust within. A man writes on a wall about the level of his own eyes, and the writing was just over six feet from the ground.

events.label: Holmes explains how he inferred the other man's age

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: If a man can stride four and a-half feet without the smallest effort, he can't be quite in the sere and yellow. That was the breadth of a puddle on the garden walk which he had evidently walked across. Patent-leather boots had gone round, and Square-toes had hopped over. I am simply applying to ordinary life a few of those precepts of observation and deduction which I advocated in that article.

events.label: Watson suggests the finger nails and the Trichinopoly

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: The finger nails and the Trichinopoly.

events.label: Holmes explains the blood writing, trimmed nail, and cigar ash

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The writing on the wall was done with a man's forefinger dipped in blood. The plaster was slightly scratched, which would not have been the case if the man's nail had been trimmed. I gathered up some scattered ash from the floor. It was dark in colour and flakey—such an ash as is only made by a Trichinopoly. I have made a special study of cigar ashes and can distinguish the ash of any known brand.

events.label: Watson asks about the florid face

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: And the florid face?

events.label: Holmes says the florid-face deduction was a daring shot and cannot be explained yet

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: That was a more daring shot, though I have no doubt that I was right. You must not ask me that at the present state of the affair.

events.label: The speaker summarizes the difficulties of the case and describes the German word RACHE as a deliberate ruse

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There is much that is still obscure, though I have quite made up my mind on the main facts. As to poor Lestrade's discovery it was simply a blind intended to put the police upon a wrong track, by suggesting Socialism and secret societies. It was not done by a German. The A, if you noticed, was printed somewhat after the German fashion. Now, a real German invariably prints in the Latin character, so that we may safely say that this was not written by one, but by a clumsy imitator who overdid his part. It was simply a ruse to divert inquiry into a wrong channel.

events.label: Watson praises Holmes's deduction

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: I shall never do that; you have brought detection as near an exact science as it ever will be brought in this world.

events.label: Holmes reacts with pleasure to Watson's praise
Holmes explains what he has inferred from the cab and the men's movements

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Patent-leathers and Square-toes came in the same cab, and they walked down the pathway together as friendly as possible—arm-in-arm, in all probability. When they got inside they walked up and down the room—or rather, Patent-leathers stood still while Square-toes walked up and down. I could read all that in the dust; and I could read that as he walked he grew more and more excited. That is shown by the increased length of his strides. He was talking all the while, and working himself up, no doubt, into a fury. Then the tragedy occurred. I've told you all I know myself now, for the rest is mere surmise and conjecture. We have a good working basis, however, on which to start. We must hurry up, for I want to go to Halle's concert to hear Norman Neruda this afternoon.

events.label: The cab travels through the streets and stops at Audley Court
Holmes and Watson arrive at Audley Court
Rance reports the night's events at the office

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: I made my report at the office.

events.label: Holmes handles a half-sovereign while asking to hear the account

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We thought that we should like to hear it all from your own lips.

events.label: Rance agrees to tell the account

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: I shall be most happy to tell you anything I can.

events.label: Rance describes his beat and the night's events

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: My time is from ten at night to six in the morning. At eleven there was a fight at the 'White Hart'; but bar that all was quiet enough on the beat. At one o'clock it began to rain, and I met Harry Murcher—him who has the Holland Grove beat—and we stood together at the corner of Henrietta Street a-talkin'. Presently—maybe about two or a little after—I thought I would take a look round and see that all was right down the Brixton Road. It was precious dirty and lonely. Not a soul did I meet all the way down, though a cab or two went past me. I was a strollin' down, thinkin' between ourselves how uncommon handy a four of gin hot would be, when suddenly the glint of a light caught my eye in the window of that same house. Now, I knew that them two houses in Lauriston Gardens was empty on account of him that owns them who won't have the drains seen to, though the very last tenant what lived in one of them died o' typhoid fever. I was knocked all in a heap therefore at seeing a light in the window, and I suspected as something was wrong. When I got to the door——

events.label: Holmes states that Rance stopped and walked back to the garden gate

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You stopped, and then walked back to the garden gate. What did you do that for?

events.label: Rance shows amazement and answers Holmes

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: Why, that's true, sir; though how you come to know it, Heaven only knows.

events.label: Rance says he wanted someone with him at the door

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: When I got up to the door it was so still and so lonesome, that I thought I'd be none the worse for some one with me. I ain't afeared of anything on this side o' the grave; but I thought that maybe it was him that died o' the typhoid inspecting the drains what killed him. The thought gave me a kind o' turn, and I walked back to the gate to see if I could see Murcher's lantern, but there wasn't no sign of him nor of anyone else.

events.label: Holmes asks whether anyone was in the street

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There was no one in the street?

events.label: Rance says the street was empty

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: Not a livin' soul, sir, nor as much as a dog.

events.label: Rance enters the house and sees a candle burning in the room
Holmes states what Rance did inside the room

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You walked round the room several times, and you knelt down by the body, and then you walked through and tried the kitchen door, and then——

events.label: Rance reacts with alarm and questions Holmes

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: Where was you hid to see all that? It seems to me that you knows a deal more than you should.

events.label: Holmes throws his card across the table to the constable
Holmes says he is one of the hounds and not the wolf

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Don't get arresting me for the murder. I am one of the hounds and not the wolf; Mr. Gregson or Mr. Lestrade will answer for that.

events.label: Holmes asks Rance what he did next

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Go on, though. What did you do next?

events.label: Rance resumes his seat

Murcher and two more arrive at the spot
Holmes asks whether the street was empty

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Was the street empty then?

events.label: Rance replies that the street was empty as far as anyone useful goes

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: Well, it was, as far as anybody that could be of any good goes.

events.label: Holmes asks what sort of man he was

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: What sort of a man was he?

events.label: Rance says the man was very drunk

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: I've seen many a drunk chap in my time, but never anyone so cryin' drunk as that cove. He was at the gate when I came out, a-leanin' up agin the railings, and a-singin' at the pitch o' his lungs about Columbine's New-fangled Banner, or some such stuff. He couldn't stand, far less help.

events.label: Rance becomes irritated at the digression
Holmes asks what the man looked like

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: His face—his dress—didn't you notice them?

events.label: Rance says he noticed the man's appearance and had to prop him up with Murcher

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: I should think I did notice them, seeing that I had to prop him up—me and Murcher between us. He was a long chap, with a red face, the lower part muffled round——

events.label: Holmes stops Rance from continuing
Holmes asks what became of the man

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: What became of him?

events.label: Rance says they did not look after the man and that he probably went home

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: We'd enough to do without lookin' after him. I'll wager he found his way home all right.

events.label: Holmes asks how the man was dressed

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: How was he dressed?

events.label: Rance answers that the man wore a brown overcoat

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: A brown overcoat.

events.label: Holmes asks whether the man had a whip in his hand

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Had he a whip in his hand?

events.label: Rance says the man had no whip

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: A whip—no.

events.label: Holmes remarks that the man must have left the whip behind
Holmes asks whether Rance saw or heard a cab after that

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You didn't happen to see or hear a cab after that?

events.label: Rance says he saw or heard no cab

communicates.speaker: john_rance
communicates.content: No.

events.label: Holmes gives Rance a half-sovereign
Holmes criticizes Rance and says he might have gained his sergeant's stripes

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I am afraid, Rance, that you will never rise in the force. That head of yours should be for use as well as ornament. You might have gained your sergeant's stripes last night. The man whom you held in your hands is the man who holds the clue of this mystery, and whom we are seeking. There is no use of arguing about it now; I tell you that it is so. Come along, Doctor.

events.label: Holmes and Watson leave for the cab together
Holmes speaks bitterly about the blundering fool and the missed opportunity

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The blundering fool. Just to think of his having such an incomparable bit of good luck, and not taking advantage of it.

events.label: Watson says he is still in the dark and questions the man's return to the house

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: I am rather in the dark still. It is true that the description of this man tallies with your idea of the second party in this mystery. But why should he come back to the house after leaving it? That is not the way of criminals.

events.label: Holmes says the man came back for the ring and that he can bait his line with it

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The ring, man, the ring: that was what he came back for. If we have no other way of catching him, we can always bait our line with the ring. I shall have him, Doctor—I'll lay you two to one that I have him. I must thank you for it all. I might not have gone but for you, and so have missed the finest study I ever came across: a study in scarlet, eh? Why shouldn't we use a little art jargon. There's the scarlet thread of murder running through the colourless skein of life, and our duty is to unravel it, and isolate it, and expose every inch of it. And now for lunch, and then for Norman Neruda. Her attack and her bowing are splendid. What's that little thing of Chopin's she plays so magnificently: Tra-la-la-lira-lira-lay.

events.label: An amateur bloodhound leans back in a cab and carols away like a lark while the narrator meditates on the many-sidedness of the human mind
The narrator meditates on the many-sidedness of the human mind
Watson lies down to sleep and fails to sleep
Holmes returns late from the concert and sits down to dinner
Holmes speaks about music and Darwin

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was magnificent. Do you remember what Darwin says about music? He claims that the power of producing and appreciating it existed among the human race long before the power of speech was arrived at. Perhaps that is why we are so subtly influenced by it. There are vague memories in our souls of those misty centuries when the world was in its childhood.

events.label: Watson says the Brixton Road affair has upset him

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: To tell the truth, it has. I ought to be more case-hardened after my Afghan experiences. I saw my own comrades hacked to pieces at Maiwand without losing my nerve.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Watson has seen the evening paper

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Have you seen the evening paper?

events.label: Holmes explains the newspaper account and points out the omitted wedding ring

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It gives a fairly good account of the affair. It does not mention the fact that when the man was raised up, a woman's wedding ring fell upon the floor. It is just as well it does not. Look at this advertisement.

events.label: Holmes sends advertisements to every paper

Holmes hands over a ring

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The man in the brown coat—our florid friend with the square toes—will come, or send an accomplice, because he would rather risk anything than lose the ring.

events.label: Watson says he has a revolver and cartridges

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: I have my old service revolver and a few cartridges.

events.label: Watson cleans and loads the revolver
Watson returns with the pistol and Holmes is scraping his violin
Holmes announces an answer to his American telegram

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The plot thickens. I have just had an answer to my American telegram. My view of the case is the correct one.

events.label: Holmes gives Watson instructions for the encounter

communicates.content: Put your pistol in your pocket. When the fellow comes speak to him in an ordinary way. Leave the rest to me. Don't frighten him by looking at him too hard.

events.label: Watson says it is eight o'clock

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: It is eight o'clock now.

events.label: Holmes says the man will probably arrive soon and gives further instructions

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: He will probably be here in a few minutes. Open the door slightly. That will do. Now put the key on the inside. Thank you!

events.label: Holmes presents a Latin book and comments on its publication date

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This is a queer old book I picked up at a stall yesterday—'De Jure inter Gentes'—published in Latin at Liege in the Lowlands, in 1642. Charles' head was still firm on his shoulders when this little brown-backed volume was struck off.

events.label: Holmes identifies the printer and speculates about William Whyte

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Philippe de Croy, whoever he may have been. I wonder who William Whyte was. Some pragmatical seventeenth century lawyer, I suppose. His writing has a legal twist about it. Here comes our man, I think.

events.label: A bell rings at the door

communicates.speaker: unknown_visitor
communicates.content: Does Dr. Watson live here?

communicates.speaker: sally_sawyer
communicates.content: It's this as has brought me, good gentlemen; a gold wedding ring in the Brixton Road. It belongs to my girl Sally... 13, Duncan Street, Houndsditch. Sally lives in lodgings at 3, Mayfield Place, Peckham. My name is Sawyer—hers is Dennis, which Tom Dennis married her.

events.label: Watson asks whether the ring is hers

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: Is that her ring?

events.label: Mrs. Sawyer confirms that the ring is Sally's and rejoices

communicates.speaker: sally_sawyer
communicates.content: The Lord be thanked! Sally will be a glad woman this night. That's the ring.

events.label: Watson returns the wedding ring to Mrs. Sawyer

Sherlock Holmes leaves and later returns unsuccessful
The maid goes to bed
The landlady passes the speaker's door on the way to bed
Holmes explains the cab chase and the disappearance

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I wouldn't have the Scotland Yarders know it for the world; I have chaffed them so much that they would never have let me hear the end of it. I can afford to laugh, because I know that I will be even with them in the long run. That creature had gone a little way when she began to limp and show every sign of being foot-sore. Presently she came to a halt, and hailed a four-wheeler which was passing. Drive to 13, Duncan Street, Houndsditch. This begins to look genuine. I hopped off before we came to the door. Nothing came out though. There was no sign or trace of his passenger. On inquiring at Number 13 we found that the house belonged to a respectable paperhanger, named Keswick, and that no one of the name either of Sawyer or Dennis had ever been heard of there. Old woman be damned! We were the old women to be so taken in. It must have been a young man, and an active one, too, besides being an incomparable actor. The get-up was inimitable. He saw that he was followed, no doubt, and used this means of giving me the slip. It shows that the man we are after is not as lonely as I imagined he was, but has friends who are ready to risk something for him. Now, Doctor, you are looking done-up. Take my advice and turn in.

events.label: Watson goes to bed and Holmes remains up playing the violin

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There's more work to be got out of one of those little beggars than out of a dozen of the force. The mere sight of an official-looking person seals men's lips. These youngsters, however, go everywhere and hear everything. They are as sharp as needles, too; all they want is organisation.

events.label: Watson asks whether Holmes is employing the boys on the Brixton case

communicates.speaker: john_watson

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Yes; there is a point which I wish to ascertain. It is merely a matter of time.

events.label: Gregson arrives at Holmes's room and congratulates Holmes

communicates.speaker: tobias_gregson
communicates.content: My dear fellow, congratulate me! I have made the whole thing as clear as day.

events.label: Holmes asks Gregson whether he is on the right track

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Do you mean that you are on the right track?

communicates.speaker: tobias_gregson
communicates.content: The right track! Why, sir, we have the man under lock and key. Arthur Charpentier, sub-lieutenant in Her Majesty's navy.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Take a seat, and try one of these cigars. We are anxious to know how you managed it. Will you have some whiskey and water?

events.label: Gregson laughs and says Lestrade is on the wrong track after Stangerson

communicates.speaker: tobias_gregson
communicates.content: The fun of it is that that fool Lestrade, who thinks himself so smart, has gone off upon the wrong track altogether. He is after the secretary Stangerson, who had no more to do with the crime than the babe unborn. I have no doubt that he has caught him by this time.

events.label: Gregson laughs until he chokes at the idea

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You remember the hat beside the dead man?

communicates.content: Have you heard of the mysterious death of your late boarder Mr. Enoch J. Cleveland? At what o'clock did Mr. Drebber leave your house for the train? Was that the last which you saw of him?

communicates.speaker: arthur_charpentier

communicates.speaker: madame_charpentier
communicates.content: I will tell you all, sir. My son is utterly innocent of it. My dread is that he may appear to be compromised.

events.label: Mrs. Charpentier tells the account of Mr. Drebber and Mr. Stangerson staying and behaving badly

communicates.speaker: mrs_charpentier
communicates.content: I had no intention of telling you all this, but since my poor daughter has disclosed it I have no alternative. Having once decided to speak, I will tell you all without omitting any particular. Mr. Drebber has been with us nearly three weeks. He and his secretary, Mr. Stangerson, had been travelling on the Continent. I noticed a "Copenhagen" label upon each of their trunks, showing that that had been their last stopping place. Stangerson was a quiet reserved man, but his employer was coarse in his habits and brutish in his ways. The very night of his arrival he became very much the worse for drink, and after twelve o'clock in the day he could hardly ever be said to be sober. His manners towards the maid-servants were disgustingly free and familiar. He speedily assumed the same attitude towards my daughter, Alice, and spoke to her more than once in a way which she is too innocent to understand. On one occasion he actually seized her in his arms and embraced her, an outrage which caused his own secretary to reproach him for his unmanly conduct.

events.label: Mrs. Charpentier explains why she delayed giving Mr. Drebber notice

communicates.speaker: mrs_charpentier
communicates.content: Would to God that I had given him notice on the very day that he came. It was a sore temptation. They were paying a pound a day each—fourteen pounds a week, and this is the slack season. I am a widow, and my boy in the Navy has cost me much. I grudged to lose the money. I acted for the best. This last was too much, however, and I gave him notice to leave on account of it. That was the reason of his going.

events.label: Mrs. Charpentier describes Mr. Drebber's return and proposal to Alice

communicates.speaker: mrs_charpentier
communicates.content: My heart grew light when I saw him drive away. My son is on leave just now, but I did not tell him anything of all this, for his temper is violent, and he is passionately fond of his sister. In less than an hour there was a ring at the bell, and I learned that Mr. Drebber had returned. He was much excited, and evidently the worse for drink. He forced his way into the room, where I was sitting with my daughter, and made some incoherent remark about having missed his train. He then turned to Alice, and before my very face, proposed to her that she should fly with him. 'You are of age,' he said, 'and there is no law to stop you. I have money enough and to spare. Never mind the old girl here, but come along with me now straight away. You shall live like a princess.' Poor Alice was so frightened that she shrunk away from him, but he caught her by the wrist and endeavoured to draw her towards the door.

events.label: Arthur Charpentier enters the room during the struggle with Mr. Drebber

communicates.speaker: arthur_charpentier
communicates.content: I don't think that fine fellow will trouble us again. I will just go after him and see what he does with himself.

events.label: Arthur Charpentier leaves after the altercation
Mr. Drebber's mysterious death is reported the next morning
Mrs. Charpentier speaks haltingly about her son's return and absence

communicates.speaker: mrs_charpentier
communicates.content: I do not know. He has a latch-key, and he let himself in. Yes, after you went to bed. About eleven. Yes. I do not know what he was doing during that time.

events.label: Gregson arrests Arthur Charpentier with two officers
Gregson states his theory about Charpentier and Drebber

communicates.speaker: gregson
communicates.content: He still carried the heavy stick which the mother described him as having with him when he followed Drebber. It was a stout oak cudgel. My theory is that he followed Drebber as far as the Brixton Road. There, a fresh altercation arose between them, in the course of which Drebber received a blow from the stick, in the pit of the stomach, perhaps, which killed him without leaving any mark. The night was so wet that no one was about, so Charpentier dragged the body of his victim into the empty house. As to the candle, and the blood, and the writing on the wall, and the ring, they may all be so many tricks to throw the police on to the wrong scent.

events.label: Holmes praises Gregson's progress

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Well done! Really, Gregson, you are getting along. We shall make something of you yet.

events.label: Gregson explains Arthur Charpentier's volunteered statement

communicates.speaker: gregson
communicates.content: The young man volunteered a statement, in which he said that after following Drebber some time, the latter perceived him, and took a cab in order to get away from him. On his way home he met an old shipmate, and took a long walk with him. On being asked where this old shipmate lived, he was unable to give any satisfactory reply. I think the whole case fits together uncommonly well. Lestrade had started off upon the wrong scent. I am afraid he won't make much of it. Why, by Jove, here's the very man himself!

events.label: Lestrade enters the room looking troubled
Gregson speaks triumphantly to Lestrade

communicates.speaker: gregson
communicates.content: Ah, you find it so, Mr. Lestrade! I thought you would come to that conclusion. Have you managed to find the Secretary, Mr. Joseph Stangerson?

events.label: Lestrade states that Joseph Stangerson was murdered at Halliday's Private Hotel

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: The Secretary, Mr. Joseph Stangerson, was murdered at Halliday's Private Hotel about six o'clock this morning.

events.label: Lestrade reports that he has discovered Stangerson dead in his room

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: I have just come from his room. I was the first to discover what had occurred.

events.label: Lestrade explains his earlier investigation of Stangerson and Drebber

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: I freely confess that I was of the opinion that Stangerson was concerned in the death of Drebber. This fresh development has shown me that I was completely mistaken. Full of the one idea, I set myself to find out what had become of the Secretary. They had been seen together at Euston Station about half-past eight on the evening of the third. At two in the morning Drebber had been found in the Brixton Road. I telegraphed to Liverpool, giving a description of the man, and warning them to keep a watch upon the American boats. I then set to work calling upon all the hotels and lodging-houses in the vicinity of Euston. You see, I argued that if Drebber and his companion had become separated, the natural course for the latter would be to put up somewhere in the vicinity for the night, and then to hang about the station again next morning.

events.label: Lestrade arrives at Halliday's Private Hotel and is told Stangerson is upstairs in bed

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: I asked whether a Mr. Stangerson was living there. I was told that he had been waiting for a gentleman for two days and was upstairs in bed, to be called at nine. I said I would go up and see him at once.

events.label: Lestrade discovers blood outside Stangerson's room and the room is forced open

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: I said I would go up and see him at once.

events.label: Lestrade and the Boots find Stangerson dead in the room
Lestrade identifies the dead man as Joseph Stangerson and describes the wound

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: The Boots recognized him at once as being the same gentleman who had engaged the room under the name of Joseph Stangerson. The cause of death was a deep stab in the left side, which must have penetrated the heart.

events.label: Holmes identifies the word RACHE written in blood

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The word RACHE, written in letters of blood.

events.label: Lestrade confirms Holmes's statement

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: That was it.

events.label: Lestrade describes the unknown assassin's methodical deeds

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: There was something so methodical and so incomprehensible about the deeds of this unknown assassin, that it imparted a fresh ghastliness to his crimes.

events.label: Lestrade reports that a milk boy sees a ladder at the hotel and a man descending it

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: The man was seen. A milk boy, passing on his way to the dairy, happened to walk down the lane which leads from the mews at the back of the hotel. He noticed that a ladder, which usually lay there, was raised against one of the windows of the second floor, which was wide open. After passing, he looked back and saw a man descend the ladder. He came down so quietly and openly that the boy imagined him to be some carpenter or joiner at work in the hotel. He took no particular notice of him, beyond thinking in his own mind that it was early for him to be at work. He has an impression that the man was tall, had a reddish face, and was dressed in a long, brownish coat.

events.label: Lestrade reports blood-stained water and knife marks

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: He must have stayed in the room some little time after the murder, for we found blood-stained water in the basin, where he had washed his hands, and marks on the sheets where he had deliberately wiped his knife.

events.label: Holmes asks whether anything found in the room could furnish a clue

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Did you find nothing in the room which could furnish a clue to the murderer?

events.label: Lestrade says nothing was found except the purse, telegram, and other items

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: Nothing. Stangerson had Drebber's purse in his pocket, but it seems that this was usual, as he did all the paying. There was eighty odd pounds in it, but nothing had been taken. Whatever the motives of these extraordinary crimes, robbery is certainly not one of them. There were no papers or memoranda in the murdered man's pocket, except a single telegram, dated from Cleveland about a month ago, and containing the words, 'J. H.' There was no name appended to this message.

events.label: Holmes asks whether anything else was found

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And there was nothing else?

events.label: Lestrade reports the novel, pipe, water, and pills in the room

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: Nothing of any importance. The man's novel, with which he had read himself to sleep was lying upon the bed, and his pipe was on a chair beside him. There was a glass of water on the table, and on the window-sill a small chip ointment box containing a couple of pills.

events.label: Holmes springs up in delight and declares his case complete

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The last link. My case is complete. I have now in my hands all the threads which have formed such a tangle. There are, of course, details to be filled in, but I am as certain of all the main facts, from the time that Drebber parted from Stangerson at the station, up to the discovery of the body of the latter, as if I had seen them with my own eyes. I will give you a proof of my knowledge. Could you lay your hand upon those pills?

events.label: Lestrade produces the pills, purse, and telegram and says he took them for safekeeping

communicates.speaker: lestrade
communicates.content: I have them. I took them and the purse and the telegram, intending to have them put in a place of safety at the Police Station. It was the merest chance my taking these pills, for I am bound to say that I do not attach any importance to them.

events.label: Holmes asks for the pills and questions whether they are ordinary pills

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Give them here. Now, Doctor, are those ordinary pills?

events.label: Watson states that the pills are not ordinary and describes their appearance

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: They certainly were not. They were of a pearly grey colour, small, round, and almost transparent against the light.

events.label: Watson suggests the pills are soluble in water and Holmes confirms it

communicates.speaker: john_watson
communicates.content: From their lightness and transparency, I should imagine that they are soluble in water.

events.label: Holmes asks Watson to fetch the terrier

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Now would you mind going down and fetching that poor little devil of a terrier which has been bad so long, and which the landlady wanted you to put out of its pain yesterday.

events.label: Watson carries the terrier upstairs and places it on a cushion on the rug
Holmes cuts a pill in two and dissolves half of it in water
Holmes places the dissolved pill mixture before the terrier and the terrier licks it up
The observers watch the terrier and no effect appears
Holmes exclaims that the pills suspected in Drebber's case were found after Stangerson's death and that one pill is inert

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It can't be a coincidence. The very pills which I suspected in the case of Drebber are actually found after the death of Stangerson. And yet they are inert. What can it mean? Surely my whole chain of reasoning cannot have been false. It is impossible! And yet this wretched dog is none the worse. Ah, I have it! I have it!

events.label: Holmes prepares the other pill in the same way and gives it to the terrier, which dies
Holmes states that one pill was deadly poison and the other harmless

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I should have more faith. I ought to know by this time that when a fact appears to be opposed to a long train of deductions, it invariably proves to be capable of bearing some other interpretation. Of the two pills in that box one was of the most deadly poison, and the other was entirely harmless. I ought to have known that before ever I saw the box at all.

events.label: Holmes says that the murder will not lead to more murders

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There will be no more murders.

events.label: Holmes says that he knows the assassin's name and expects to secure him shortly

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I do. ... This I expect very shortly to do.

events.label: Holmes says that the assassin is a shrewd and desperate man supported by another equally clever man

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: we have a shrewd and desperate man to deal with, who is supported, as I have had occasion to prove, by another who is as clever as himself

events.label: Wiggins enters the room and reports that the cab is downstairs

communicates.speaker: wiggins
communicates.content: Please, sir, I have the cab downstairs.

events.label: Holmes shows handcuffs and comments on their use at Scotland Yard

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Why don't you introduce this pattern at Scotland Yard? See how beautifully the spring works. They fasten in an instant.

events.label: Holmes asks the cabman to help with the boxes

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The cabman may as well help me with my boxes. Just ask him to step up, Wiggins.

events.label: Holmes handcuffs Jefferson Hope and reveals his identity

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Gentlemen, let me introduce you to Mr. Jefferson Hope, the murderer of Enoch Drebber and of Joseph Stangerson.

events.label: Jefferson Hope breaks free and leaps through the window
Holmes states that they have Hope's cab and that it will take him to Scotland Yard

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We have his cab. It will serve to take him to Scotland Yard.

events.label: Holmes says the mystery has reached its end and invites questions

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We have reached the end of our little mystery. You are very welcome to put any questions that you like to me now, and there is no danger that I will refuse to answer them.

events.label: A desert region lies across the central North American continent
The Great Alkali Plain has barrenness, inhospitality, and misery
Pawnees and Blackfeet traverse the land
Wild animals move through the wilderness
A pathway runs across the desert and is marked by bones
A solitary traveller stands on the plain on May 4, 1847
A man toils up from a ravine to a little elevation in search of water.
The man looks over the barren landscape and sees no signs of moisture.
The man sits down in the shelter of a boulder.
The man deposits his rifle and grey shawl bundle on the ground.
A crying child emerges from the grey shawl bundle after it is lowered.
The little girl complains that she has been hurt.

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: You've hurt me!

events.label: The man unwraps the grey shawl and lifts out a little girl.
The man answers the girl's question about her hurt head.

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: Mother's gone. I guess you'll see her before long.

events.label: The little girl says her mother did not say good-bye and asks whether there is water or food.

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: Funny, she didn't say good-bye; she 'most always did if she was just goin' over to Auntie's for tea, and now she's been away three days. Say, it's awful dry, ain't it? Ain't there no water, nor nothing to eat?

events.label: The man replies that there is nothing and tells the girl to be patient.

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: No, there ain't nothing, dearie. You'll just need to be patient awhile, and then you'll be all right. Put your head up agin me like that, and then you'll feel bullier. It ain't easy to talk when your lips is like leather, but I guess I'd best let you know how the cards lie.

events.label: The little girl shows two glittering pieces of mica.
The little girl says she will give the mica to Brother Bob when they return home.

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: When we goes back to home I'll give them to brother Bob.

events.label: The man says the girl will soon see prettier things.

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: You'll see prettier things than them soon. You just wait a bit.

events.label: The man explains that the party left the river, expected another river, but the navigation was wrong and the water ran out.

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: I was going to tell you though—you remember when we left the river? Well, we reckoned we'd strike another river soon, d'ye see. But there was somethin' wrong; compasses, or map, or somethin', and it didn't turn up. Water ran out. Just except a little drop for the likes of you and—and——

events.label: The little girl comments that the man could not wash himself.

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: And you couldn't wash yourself.

events.label: The man says there was no water to wash or drink and names the dead members of the party.

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: No, nor drink. And Mr. Bender, he was the fust to go, and then Indian Pete, and then Mrs. McGregor, and then Johnny Hones, and then, dearie, your mother.

events.label: The man carries the child while the pair tramps onward
The child asks whether they are going to die too

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: Do you mean that we are going to die too?

events.label: The child laughs and says they will be with mother again when they die

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: Why didn't you say so before? You gave me such a fright. Why, of course, now as long as we die we'll be with mother again.

events.label: The man answers that the child will be with mother again

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: Yes, you will, dearie.

events.label: The child says she will tell mother how good the man has been and imagines a welcome in Heaven

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: And you too. I'll tell her how awful good you've been. I'll bet she meets us at the door of Heaven with a big pitcher of water, and a lot of buckwheat cakes, hot, and toasted on both sides, like Bob and me was fond of. How long will it be first?

events.label: The man answers that he does not know and that it will not be very long

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: I don't know—not very long.

events.label: The man looks toward the northern horizon
Three specks appear and become three large brown birds that settle on rocks near the wanderers
The birds are identified as buzzards
The child points at the birds and claps her hands
The child asks whether God made this country

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: Say, did God make this country?

events.label: The man answers that God made the country in Illinois and Missouri

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: In course He did. He made the country down in Illinois, and He made the Missouri.

events.label: The child says somebody else made this country and that water and trees were forgotten

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: I guess somebody else made the country in these parts. It's not nearly so well done. They forgot the water and the trees.

events.label: The man suggests offering up prayer

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: What would ye think of offering up prayer?

events.label: The child says it is not night yet

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: It ain't night yet.

events.label: The man says it does not matter and asks her to say the prayers used in the wagon on the Plains

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: It don't matter. It ain't quite regular, but He won't mind that, you bet. You say over them ones that you used to say every night in the waggon when we was on the Plains.

events.label: The child asks why the man does not say some himself

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: Why don't you say some yourself?

events.label: The man says he has forgotten the prayers and has not said any since he was a child

communicates.speaker: man
communicates.content: I disremember them. I hain't said none since I was half the height o' that gun. I guess it's never too late. You say them out, and I'll stand by and come in on the choruses.

events.label: The child lays out the shawl for kneeling and instructs the man how to pray

communicates.speaker: little_girl
communicates.content: Then you'll need to kneel down, and me too. You've got to put your hands up like this. It makes you feel kind o' good.

events.label: The two wanderers kneel side by side on the shawl and pray
The child finishes the prayer and the pair resumes sitting until the child falls asleep on the man's breast
The man watches over the child and then falls asleep beside her
A great caravan approaches the bluff and stops below it
The caravan leaders hold a short council
One man says the wells are to the right

communicates.speaker: stangerson
communicates.content: The wells are to the right, my brothers.

events.label: Another man says the route to the Rio Grande lies to the right of the Sierra Blanco

communicates.speaker: stangerson
communicates.content: To the right of the Sierra Blanco—so we shall reach the Rio Grande.

events.label: A third man declares that their people will not be abandoned

communicates.speaker: stangerson
communicates.content: Fear not for water. He who could draw it from the rocks will not now abandon His own chosen people.

events.label: The caravan members shout amen
A young man points toward the crag above them
The caravan halts and prepares weapons at the sight of the pink signal
Young men dismount and climb the steep slope
The scout group reaches the top and sees something startling
John Ferrier and a little girl sleep beside a boulder on a plateau
Buzzards scream and fly away when newcomers appear
The cries of the buzzards wake the two sleepers
John Ferrier stands up and looks over the plain at the large moving party
John Ferrier mutters that the situation is what they call delirium

communicates.speaker: john_ferrier
communicates.content: This is what they call delirium, I guess.

events.label: The child stands beside John Ferrier and looks around silently
The rescuing party convinces the two castaways that their appearance is real
Rescuers lift Lucy Ferrier onto a shoulder and support John Ferrier toward the wagons
John Ferrier names himself and explains that only he and the girl remain alive from twenty-one people

communicates.speaker: john_ferrier
communicates.content: My name is John Ferrier; me and that little un are all that's left o' twenty-one people. The rest is all dead o' thirst and hunger away down in the south.

events.label: Someone asks whether the girl is John Ferrier's child

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: Is she your child?

events.label: John Ferrier declares that Lucy is his and renames her Lucy Ferrier

communicates.speaker: john_ferrier
communicates.content: I guess she is now; she's mine 'cause I saved her. No man will take her from me. She's Lucy Ferrier from this day on.

events.label: John Ferrier asks the rescuers who they are and comments on their number

communicates.speaker: john_ferrier
communicates.content: Who are you, though? there seems to be a powerful lot of ye.

events.label: A rescuer states that the group numbers nearly ten thousand and identifies the Mormons

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: Nigh upon ten thousand. We are the persecuted children of God—the chosen of the Angel Merona.

events.label: John Ferrier says he has never heard of the Angel Merona and remarks on the crowd

communicates.speaker: john_ferrier
communicates.content: I never heard tell on him. He appears to have chosen a fair crowd of ye.

events.label: A rescuer warns John Ferrier not to jest about what is sacred

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: Do not jest at that which is sacred.

events.label: A rescuer explains the group's beliefs, origin in Nauvoo, and search for refuge

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: We are of those who believe in those sacred writings, drawn in Egyptian letters on plates of beaten gold, which were handed unto the holy Joseph Smith at Palmyra. We have come from Nauvoo, in the State of Illinois, where we had founded our temple. We have come to seek a refuge from the violent man and from the godless, even though it be the heart of the desert.

events.label: John Ferrier recognizes the group as Mormons

communicates.speaker: john_ferrier
communicates.content: I see, you are the Mormons.

events.label: John Ferrier asks where the group is going and the rescuer answers that they do not know and must go before their Prophet

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: We do not know. The hand of God is leading us under the person of our Prophet. You must come before him. He shall say what is to be done with you.

events.label: The escort reaches the base of the hill and the crowd gathers around the castaways
The escort and crowd move on toward a large ornate wagon
The leader sits by the driver reading a brown-backed volume and listens to the account
The leader turns to the two castaways
The leader sets terms for taking Ferrier and the child with the Mormons.

communicates.speaker: stangerson
communicates.content: If we take you with us, it can only be as believers in our own creed. We shall have no wolves in our fold. Better far that your bones should bleach in this wilderness than that you should prove to be that little speck of decay which in time corrupts the whole fruit. Will you come with us on these terms?

events.label: Ferrier agrees to come with the Mormons on any terms.

communicates.speaker: john_ferrier
communicates.content: Guess I'll come with you on any terms.

events.label: The leader orders Brother Stangerson to take Ferrier, feed them, and teach the creed.

communicates.speaker: stangerson
communicates.content: Take him, Brother Stangerson, give him food and drink, and the child likewise. Let it be your task also to teach him our holy creed. We have delayed long enough. Forward! On, on to Zion!

events.label: The crowd of Mormons repeats the cry to go on to Zion.

communicates.speaker: the_mormon_caravan
communicates.content: On, on to Zion!

events.label: The caravan starts moving again.
The Elder leads Ferrier and the child to his wagon and provides a meal.
The Elder tells Ferrier and the child that they will remain in the wagon, recover, and be of the Mormon religion.

communicates.speaker: stangerson
communicates.content: You shall remain here. In a few days you will have recovered from your fatigues. In the meantime, remember that now and for ever you are of our religion. Brigham Young has said it, and he has spoken with the voice of Joseph Smith, which is the voice of God.

events.label: Young administers the settlement and plans the future city
The immigrant Mormons reach the Utah valley

communicates.speaker: young
communicates.content: this was the promised land, and that these virgin acres were to be theirs for evermore

events.label: John Ferrier and Lucy Ferrier accompany the Mormons to the end of the pilgrimage
John Ferrier receives a tract of land
John Ferrier builds a log-house on his farm
John Ferrier improves and tills his lands
John Ferrier refuses to set up a female establishment
John Ferrier remains strictly celibate
Lucy Ferrier grows up in the log-house and assists John Ferrier
Lucy Ferrier grows taller and stronger over the years
Lucy Ferrier rides into the city on a commission from her father
Lucy Ferrier reaches the outskirts of the city and finds the road blocked by a cattle drove
Lucy Ferrier tries to pass the blockade by pushing her horse into a gap
The cattle close in behind Lucy Ferrier and she becomes surrounded by the moving herd
Lucy Ferrier urges her horse forward to force a path through the cattle
A bullock's horns strike the flank of the mustang and excite it to madness
The horse rears and tosses violently
The excited horse continues to plunge and threaten Lucy Ferrier
Lucy Ferrier grows dizzy, loosens her grip, and struggles to remain in the saddle
A kindly voice at Lucy Ferrier's elbow assures her of assistance

communicates.speaker: jefferson_hope
communicates.content: assistance

events.label: Jefferson Hope catches the frightened horse by the curb and brings Lucy Ferrier through the drove
Jefferson Hope speaks to Lucy Ferrier and asks whether she is hurt

communicates.speaker: jefferson_hope
communicates.content: You're not hurt, I hope, miss

events.label: Lucy Ferrier looks up at Jefferson Hope and laughs
Lucy Ferrier speaks to Jefferson Hope and says she is frightened and that Poncho was scared by the cows

communicates.speaker: lucy_ferrier
communicates.content: I'm awful frightened; whoever would have thought that Poncho would have been so scared by a lot of cows?

events.label: John Ferrier sits with Lucy Ferrier and they discuss their situation

communicates.speaker: john_ferrier
communicates.content: Don't you scare yourself. We'll fix it up somehow or another. You don't find your fancy kind o' lessening for this chap, do you? No; of course not. I shouldn't care to hear you say you did. He's a likely lad, and he's a Christian, which is more than these folk here, in spite o' all their praying and preaching. There's a party starting for Nevada to-morrow, and I'll manage to send him a message letting him know the hole we are in. If I know anything o' that young man, he'll be back here with a speed that would whip electro-telegraphs. When he comes, he will advise us for the best. But it is for you that I am frightened, dear. One hears—one hears such dreadful stories about those who oppose the Prophet: something terrible always happens to them. But we haven't opposed him yet. It will be time to look out for squalls when we do. We have a clear month before us; at the end of that, I guess we had best shin out of Utah. Leave Utah! That's about the size of it. But the farm? We will raise as much as we can in money, and let the rest go. To tell the truth, Lucy, it isn't the first time I have thought of doing it. I don't care about knuckling under to any man, as these folk do to their darned prophet. I'm a free-born American, and it's all new to me. Guess I'm too old to learn. If he comes browsing about this farm, he might chance to run up against a charge of buckshot travelling in the opposite direction. But they won't let us leave. Wait till Jefferson comes, and we'll soon manage that. In the meantime, don't you fret yourself, my dearie, and don't get your eyes swelled up, else he'll be walking into me when he sees you. There's nothing to be afeared about, and there's no danger at all.

events.label: Holmes explains reasoning backwards and contrasts analytic and synthetic reasoning

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have already explained to you that what is out of the common is usually a guide rather than a hindrance. In solving a problem of this sort, the grand thing is to be able to reason backwards. That is a very useful accomplishment, and a very easy one, but people do not practise it much. In the every-day affairs of life it is more useful to reason forwards, and so the other comes to be neglected. There are fifty who can reason synthetically for one who can reason analytically. I hardly expected that you would. Let me see if I can make it clearer. Most people, if you describe a train of events to them, will tell you what the result would be. They can put those events together in their minds, and argue from them that something will come to pass. There are few people, however, who, if you told them a result, would be able to evolve from their own inner consciousness what the steps were which led up to that result. This power is what I mean when I talk of reasoning backwards, or analytically.

events.label: Holmes explains the steps of his reasoning from the cab tracks and garden path

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Now this was a case in which you were given the result and had to find everything else for yourself. Now let me endeavour to show you the different steps in my reasoning. To begin at the beginning. I approached the house, as you know, on foot, and with my mind entirely free from all impressions. I naturally began by examining the roadway, and there, as I have already explained to you, I saw clearly the marks of a cab, which, I ascertained by inquiry, must have been there during the night. I satisfied myself that it was a cab and not a private carriage by the narrow gauge of the wheels. The ordinary London growler is considerably less wide than a gentleman's brougham. This was the first point gained. I then walked slowly down the garden path, which happened to be composed of a clay soil, peculiarly suitable for taking impressions. No doubt it appeared to you to be a mere trampled line of slush, but to my trained eyes every mark upon its surface had a meaning. There is no branch of detective science which is so important and so much neglected as the art of tracing footsteps. Happily, I have always laid great stress upon it, and much practice has made it second nature to me. I saw the heavy footmarks of the constables, but I saw also the track of the two men who had first passed through the garden. It was easy to tell that they had been before the others, because in places their marks had been entirely obliterated by the others coming upon the top of them. In this way my second link was formed, which told me that the nocturnal visitors were two in number, one remarkable for his height, and the other fashionably dressed.
